blueprintPlan.intentSummary: Topic: choosing tiles for a home renovation. Audience: homeowners planning a renovation. Objective: help homeowners understand how different tile choices can affect the finished result and make a more informed selection. Business: generic tile retailer. Format: short-form social video.
blueprintPlan.structuralApproach: Open with a bold dual-contrast claim about tile choice outcomes, then hold the decision constant (same room type) while alternating between a mismatched tile choice and a well-matched one, reinforced by synchronized on-screen text, closing with a single visual break and pause before a guidance-seeking call to action.

scenes.purpose: Hook the audience with a broad claim that tile choice changes the finished look and feel of a room.
scenes.contentInstruction: State a generalized contrast between two different finished outcomes that can result from tile choice, without yet naming specific tiles or rooms, to create anticipation.
scenes.visual: Show a quick establishing shot of a renovation space, neutral and unbranded.
scenes.text: Short on-screen phrase mirroring the spoken contrast claim.
scenes.speech: Deliver the opening contrast claim in a confident, clear tone.
scenes.pacing: Single continuous shot, fast entry, no cuts.

mandatoryPoints.text: different tile choices can create different finished outcomes

mechanisms.principle: Open with a bold, generalized dual-contrast claim before any explanation, prompting the audience to want resolution of the comparison.

scenes.purpose: Show the mismatched tile outcome for a specific room/use case.
scenes.contentInstruction: Present one room/use case and demonstrate the negative consequence of an unsuitable tile choice for that context (e.g. durability, moisture, style mismatch), keeping the room constant for later contrast.
requiredInformation: to be supplied: specific example room and tile type to illustrate mismatch
scenes.visual: Show the chosen room type with a tile finish that visibly clashes with its function.
scenes.text: On-screen caption naming the issue caused by the mismatch, synced to narration.
scenes.speech: Explain plainly why this tile choice underperforms in this context.
scenes.transition: Cut to matched version in next section.

mandatoryPoints.text: suitability depends on the room/use case

mechanisms.principle: Structure a narrative by alternating between two opposing behavioral outcomes tied to the same subject, reinforcing a before/after or type-A/type-B dichotomy.
Pair spoken narration with synchronized on-screen text restating the same content to reinforce the message through a parallel visual channel.

limitations: Specific tile examples not supplied by intent

scenes.purpose: Show the well-matched tile outcome for the same room/use case.
scenes.contentInstruction: Return to the same room/use case and show the positive outcome achieved with a well-suited tile choice, directly opposing section 2's outcome.
requiredInformation: to be supplied: matching tile example for the same room
scenes.visual: Show the same room type with a tile finish appropriate to its function and aesthetic.
scenes.text: On-screen caption naming the benefit of the matched choice, synced to narration.
scenes.speech: Explain plainly why this tile choice works well in this context.
scenes.transition: Move into a second room example to broaden the point.

mandatoryPoints.text: different tile choices can create different finished outcomes
suitability depends on the room/use case

mechanisms.principle: Structure a narrative by alternating between two opposing behavioral outcomes tied to the same subject, reinforcing a before/after or type-A/type-B dichotomy.
Pair spoken narration with synchronized on-screen text restating the same content to reinforce the message through a parallel visual channel.

scenes.purpose: Repeat the mismatch versus match contrast with a second, different room/use case to generalize the principle.
scenes.contentInstruction: Briefly show a second room/use case with the same mismatch-versus-match pairing, more quickly than sections 2-3, to reinforce that suitability depends on context rather than one universal best tile.
requiredInformation: to be supplied: second example room and tile pairing
scenes.visual: Split or sequential shots contrasting the two outcomes in the new room type.
scenes.text: Short synced captions labeling each outcome.
scenes.speech: Summarize the same mismatch/match logic applied to the new context.
scenes.pacing: Slightly faster cadence than sections 2-3, still single continuous shots.
scenes.transition: Move to a summarizing principle statement.

mandatoryPoints.text: suitability depends on the room/use case

mechanisms.principle: Structure a narrative by alternating between two opposing behavioral outcomes tied to the same subject, reinforcing a before/after or type-A/type-B dichotomy.
Pair spoken narration with synchronized on-screen text restating the same content to reinforce the message through a parallel visual channel.

scenes.purpose: Derive a practical selection principle from the preceding comparisons.
scenes.contentInstruction: State the general rule that emerges from the contrasts: the right tile choice depends on the specific room and its use, not on any single tile being universally best.
scenes.visual: Neutral shot summarizing the space, perhaps a wider view of multiple tile samples.
scenes.text: On-screen summary line matching the spoken principle.
scenes.speech: Deliver the takeaway rule in a calm, instructive tone.

mandatoryPoints.text: suitability depends on the room/use case

mechanisms.principle: Pair spoken narration with synchronized on-screen text restating the same content to reinforce the message through a parallel visual channel.

scenes.purpose: Mark closure of the educational content with a visual break before the call to action.
scenes.contentInstruction: Introduce a single clean cut to a new shot signalling the piece is wrapping up, with a brief pause in narration.
scenes.visual: Cut to a calmer, final framing, e.g. a tidy finished space or product display.
scenes.text: Minimal or no text, allowing the pause to register visually.
scenes.speech: Pause briefly after the previous statement before the final line.
scenes.transition: Lead directly into the call to action.

mechanisms.principle: Maintain an unbroken visual continuity through most of a piece, then mark closure with a single cut and pauses to signal an ending.

scenes.purpose: Invite the audience to seek personalized guidance before finalizing their tile choice.
scenes.contentInstruction: Encourage the audience to visit the showroom or contact the business for guidance tailored to their specific room and needs, framed as helpful rather than pressuring.
requiredInformation: to be supplied: showroom location or contact method
scenes.visual: Simple closing shot, calm framing consistent with section 6.
scenes.text: Short on-screen prompt reinforcing the spoken call to action.
scenes.speech: Deliver the invitation in a warm, low-pressure tone.
scenes.pacing: Slow final pace with a closing pause.
scenes.cta: Prompt the viewer to visit the showroom or contact the business for personalized guidance on choosing tiles.

mandatoryPoints.text: customers can seek guidance before choosing

elementClasses.reason: Scene order and timing come from the blueprint and are laid out on the timeline.
The footage you supply becomes real video clips placed at each scene’s start.
Each clip is trimmed to its scene; the trim values are real and editable in the editor.
Speed is one of the editor’s own clip properties (only used when you pick it, or when a short clip is stretched).
A real, editable text overlay that holds the blueprint’s instruction. It is a placeholder to replace, not final copy.
A real, editable text overlay for the call to action, created only for scenes the blueprint marks as carrying one.
The blueprint gives plain-language direction and the editor has five fixed transition types, so no automatic mapping is made. Clips start as cuts; the direction is kept in the scene’s notes.
The blueprint’s speech direction is kept as an instruction. No voice is generated; you record or upload audio.
No music is selected or generated; you add an audio track in the editor.
The editor can transcribe and caption, but assembly does not create captions.
Editable in the editor, not generated here. Note: the current export button does not yet send lower thirds.
Editable in the editor, not generated here. Note: the current export button does not yet send shapes.
The reference video’s own footage is never reused: a reconstruction applies its principles to your media, it does not copy it.
Text burned into the reference’s frames is flattened pixels, not a separate element, and is not copied or re-created as editable text.
Graphics and logos baked into the reference’s frames cannot be separated from the picture.
The reference’s colour treatment is baked into its pixels and is not extracted as editable settings.
Effects and filters applied to the reference are baked in and cannot be recovered as editable effects.
The reference’s mixed audio cannot be split back into editable tracks.

issues.message: 8 text placeholders are in the draft. They are real text overlays: replace or delete them before exporting, or their instruction text will be rendered into the video.
